name: Sicilian: Hyperaccelerated Dragon
summary: The Hyperaccelerated Dragon (2...g6) fianchettoes at once, delaying ...Nc6 to finesse move orders within the Dragon family.
intro: The Hyperaccelerated Dragon begins 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g6, developing the kingside bishop immediately and postponing ...Nc6. By delaying the knight move, Black keeps maximum flexibility, hoping to reach a favourable version of the Accelerated Dragon or to sidestep certain White setups. It is best understood as a move-order finesse within the broader Dragon and Accelerated Dragon complex rather than a fully independent opening.
line: e4 c5 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The point of 2...g6 is subtlety of move order rather than a change of pawn structure. Black intends the same kingside fianchetto as in the Dragon and Accelerated Dragon, placing the bishop on g7 to bear down the long dark diagonal toward White's centre and queenside. By not committing the b8-knight to c6 yet, Black keeps the option of meeting an eventual c4 (the Maróczy Bind) with ...Nf6 and ...d6, or of choosing a different piece arrangement according to White's plan. The trade-off is that the early, non-central second move grants White some independent tries that an immediate ...Nc6 or ...d6 would deny.

In the main lines the position usually transposes to Accelerated Dragon territory once ...Nc6 and ...Nf6 appear, so the strategic themes are familiar: Black seeks the freeing ...d5 break, pressure along the c-file, and active piece play, while White chooses between the space-gaining Maróczy Bind with c4 and the sharp Open Sicilian setups with Be3, f3 and a kingside pawn storm. Because Black has delayed ...Nc6, some Maróczy structures arise in a slightly different form, and Black must stay alert to White's fourth-move alternatives to the standard recapture on d4.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7, the critical continuation is 5.c4, when White erects the Maróczy Bind and Black replies ...Nc6 or ...Nf6 heading for standard bind positions. White's independent options are what give the move order its character: 3.c3 aims for a broad centre with d4 in one move, when 3...d5 or 3...Bg7 lead to Alapin-flavoured play, and an early Bc4 targets f7 before Black can react. Black must be ready to meet these tries, since the whole purpose of 2...g6 is to reach a good version rather than to walk into a poor one.

If White adopts a standard Open Sicilian development, the game typically transposes to the Accelerated Dragon after ...Nc6, or to a normal Dragon should Black later choose ...d6 and ...Nf6. The unifying aim behind Black's play is the freeing ...d5 advance, carried out under the most favourable circumstances, which frees the position and neutralises White's central pull. The choice between these transpositions is exactly what the flexible second move is designed to keep open, letting Black steer toward the structure that best answers White's chosen setup.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Hyperaccelerated Dragon, sometimes called the Accelerated Fianchetto or simply the 2...g6 Sicilian, grew out of the broader development of the Dragon and Accelerated Dragon during the twentieth century. As theory on the Maróczy Bind matured, players looked for move orders that would either avoid the bind or reach its most palatable versions, and the immediate 2...g6 became one such tool. It has been used by many grandmasters as a practical, comparatively low-theory route into Dragon-style positions, valued for its flexibility rather than for any independent attacking punch. Because so many lines transpose, it is regarded as a finesse within the Sicilian Dragon family rather than a wholly separate opening.
